events.headline: Ukraine defies Trump to resume attacks on Russian oil refineries
events.why: Ukraine has resumed attacks on Russian oil refineries after a local ceasefire in Oleshky ended, despite US pressure. India imports most of its crude, so disruption to Russian oil facilities could affect global fuel supply and prices.
implications: Damage to Russian refineries could reduce Russia's output of petrol, diesel and other fuels, which may tighten global fuel supplies and raise prices that Indian refiners and importers face.
The Kremlin says Kyiv is ignoring US wishes, which suggests Washington's efforts to restrain attacks on energy sites are not working. That may prolong uncertainty over energy flows.

exposure.reason: The channel is indirect: Indian refiners buy crude on global markets, where Russian supply matters. The reports mention no price or supply change yet, so the effect on household fuel is uncertain.

horizon.reason: Any effect on global fuel prices would depend on how much Russian refining capacity is actually damaged and how long the strikes continue.

confidence.reason: This rests on a single Guardian report that quotes a Kremlin statement; the strikes on two oil sites are described as reported and have not been independently confirmed.

affected.effect: If Russian refinery output falls, global fuel prices could rise, and Indian refiners' higher costs could eventually feed through to petrol and diesel prices.
Indian buyers of Russian crude and fuel could face supply or pricing uncertainty if attacks damage Russian oil facilities or export logistics.

watch.what: Confirmation of damage and lost output at the two Russian oil sites reportedly struck
watch.why: It would show whether the attacks are large enough to affect Russian fuel supply and global prices.

watch.what: Any US response to Ukraine's resumed refinery attacks
watch.why: It would show whether Washington will apply further pressure on Kyiv, which could change the pace of strikes.

context: India imports most of its crude oil, and Russian crude has been a significant part of its supply in recent years. Attacks on energy sites in either country can therefore matter to Indian refiners.

terms.meaning: US congressional elections held roughly halfway through a president's four-year term, which can shape how Washington handles foreign policy issues such as the war in Ukraine.

escalation.development: Ukraine has resumed attacks on Russian oil refineries after a ceasefire in the occupied town of Oleshky ended on Sunday night, with strikes reported on two oil sites.
escalation.evidence: Strikes on oil refineries are the same kind of attack on critical infrastructure that placed the war at rung 6 on 18 October. No new action at a higher rung is reported.

next_signals.signal: Either side announces general mobilisation or launches a combined offensive across the whole front, alongside the continuing strikes on energy infrastructure.
A halt to strikes on energy sites takes effect and attacks on power and oil facilities are reported to have stopped.

events.headline: Iran and US explore diplomacy amid rising threats of war
events.why: Iran says it could reopen the Strait of Hormuz in a shorter period if its conditions are met, while US President Donald Trump says the US still has targets to 'take care of'. India depends on Gulf shipping for energy.
implications: The report does not set out Iran's conditions, so the timing of any return to normal shipping through the strait remains uncertain for Indian importers and refiners.
Talks running alongside threats of war mean the situation could move either way, and prolonged disruption could raise costs for Indian refiners and fuel distributors.

exposure.reason: The strait could affect crude oil and LPG shipments to India, which are household essentials and top imports. This channel is inferred, because the report itself does not name specific cargoes.

horizon.reason: The timing depends on whether diplomacy produces a reopening and on how quickly any change in shipping and prices passes through to Indian fuel markets.

confidence.reason: This rests on a single Al Jazeera report, and Iran's conditions, the current state of the strait and the outcome of talks are not confirmed.

affected.effect: If shipping through Hormuz stays restricted, import costs for crude and gas could rise and may eventually feed into petrol, diesel and cooking gas prices; a reopening could ease this.
Uncertainty over passage through the strait could raise freight and insurance costs for traders whose cargoes pass through the Gulf.

watch.what: Iran setting out the conditions under which it would reopen the Strait of Hormuz, or announcing a reopening
watch.why: It would show whether shipping through the strait could resume and how soon.

watch.what: Further US statements or action on the targets Trump says the US still has to 'take care of'
watch.why: It would show whether talks are holding or tensions are escalating toward war.

context: India imports most of its crude oil, and much of its crude and liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) comes from Gulf producers whose cargoes ship through Hormuz.
Disruption to a major shipping route usually raises oil prices, freight rates and insurance costs, even before physical supplies fall.

terms.meaning: The Strait of Hormuz is a narrow waterway linking the Gulf to the open sea, through which a large share of the world's oil exports passes.

cause.text: It is not yet known why the strait is closed.

flows.india_link: A large share of the crude oil India imports from the Gulf is shipped through the Strait of Hormuz, so disruption there can raise India's fuel import costs.
Much of India's liquefied natural gas from Qatar and the UAE passes through the strait, supplying power plants, fertiliser makers and city gas networks.

events.headline: Russia opens terrorism case over Ukraine oil refinery attack
events.why: Russia has opened a terrorism case after a large drone attack reportedly caused significant damage to a refinery that Ukraine called one of Russia's largest. Any effect on India would be indirect, through global oil and fuel prices.
implications: If the damage cuts the refinery's output, less Russian fuel could reach export markets, which may tighten global supplies of refined products and push international prices up.
Higher international fuel prices could raise costs for Indian oil companies and importers, although the report gives no estimate of how long the refinery may be out of action.

exposure.reason: The report describes no direct link to India. Any effect would come indirectly through global fuel prices if the refinery's output falls, and the report does not say whether it will.

horizon.reason: Any change in global fuel prices would depend on how long the refinery stays damaged, and such shifts usually reach Indian importers over several weeks rather than days.

confidence.reason: This rests on a single ABC News report, and the extent of the damage is described as reported and relies on Ukraine's description of the facility.

affected.effect: If lost refinery output tightens global fuel supplies, higher international prices could eventually feed into the cost of fuel in India, but the report does not say this will happen.

watch.what: Official confirmation of how badly the refinery was damaged and whether its output has been halted
watch.why: It would show whether any meaningful volume of Russian fuel is likely to leave global supply.

watch.what: Further drone attacks on Russian oil refineries
watch.why: Repeated strikes would raise the chance of a lasting reduction in Russian refined fuel supply to world markets.

context: India imports most of the crude oil it uses, so Indian fuel costs are sensitive to global prices of crude oil and refined fuels.
A refinery turns crude oil into petrol, diesel and other fuels, so damage to one can reduce fuel supply even when crude oil supplies are unaffected.

events.headline: Somali piracy resurges as Iranian vessel seized carrying 23 crew
events.why: Somali pirates have seized an Iranian fishing vessel with 23 people aboard, and a European Union maritime security body warns it could become a base for further attacks. Indian trade and seafarers use these Indian Ocean routes.
implications: If the captured vessel is used to attack merchant ships, shipowners may pay more for insurance and security on Arabian Sea routes, and those costs could eventually reach Indian importers and exporters.
Indian crews serve on many merchant ships, so any attack on a commercial vessel near this lane could put Indian seafarers at risk.

exposure.reason: The reports describe only one seizure of a fishing vessel, with no disruption to merchant ships yet. India's sea trade could be affected through shipping lane risk and insurance costs, so exposure is medium.

horizon.reason: Any effect on freight costs or voyages depends on whether the pirates use the captured vessel to attack merchant ships in the coming weeks.

confidence.reason: The report from the South China Morning Post relies on an official statement from the European Union's MSCIO, but it is a single outlet and no further attacks are confirmed.

affected.effect: If pirates threaten the commercial lane, shipowners and insurers may charge more for cargo moving across the Arabian Sea, which could raise costs for Indian importers and exporters.
Indian seafarers working on merchant ships passing through the area could face greater risk if the captured vessel is used for further attacks.

watch.what: Any further seizure or attack on a commercial ship near the shipping lane the captured vessel is approaching
watch.why: It would show whether the warning about a floating base for further attacks is coming true.
watch.where: European Union Maritime Security Centre Indian Ocean (MSCIO)

context: India imports most of its crude oil and carries most of its trade by sea, much of it across the Arabian Sea and near the Gulf of Aden.
Pirates often use a hijacked fishing vessel as a floating base, because it lets them operate farther from the coast while looking like ordinary traffic.

terms.meaning: The European Union's Maritime Security Centre Indian Ocean, a body that monitors threats to shipping in the region and issues warnings to the industry.

escalation.development: Somali pirates seized an Iranian fishing vessel with 23 people aboard, and the European Union's MSCIO warned that it could be used as a base for further attacks.
escalation.evidence: The seizure of a single fishing vessel is a limited attack. The reports describe no repeated or sustained attacks on merchant ships, so the level stays where it is.

next_signals.signal: Repeated attacks or seizures of commercial ships in the shipping lane, launched from the captured vessel or others, would show a move to sustained strikes.

events.headline: Beijing ramps up maritime patrols around Taiwan, prompting Taipei to shadow ships
events.why: The South China Morning Post reports that Beijing has stepped up coastguard patrols around Taiwan, from its eastern approaches to waters near Quemoy and Dongsha Island, and Taipei is shadowing the ships. India is affected only if shipping or trade through these waters is disturbed.
implications: The reports describe patrols and shadowing only, with no attacks or disruption to commercial shipping. Any effect on India would therefore depend on whether the pressure later interferes with merchant vessels or port access.

If shipping insurers or carriers see these waters as riskier, freight costs and delivery times for Indian importers of electronics and components from East Asia could rise. This is an inference, not something the reports state.

exposure.reason: The reports describe only patrols and shadowing of ships, with no disruption to trade or shipping lanes. Any channel into India, such as freight costs or component supply, is indirect and would need further escalation.

horizon.reason: No disruption to trade is reported, so any effect on Indian supply chains would appear only if the patrols later interfere with commercial shipping.

confidence.reason: This rests on a single outlet, the South China Morning Post, with no official statement from Beijing or Taipei quoted in the summary, so the scale of the deployment is unconfirmed.

affected.effect: Indian importers of East Asian electronics could face higher freight or insurance costs if the patrols begin to disrupt commercial shipping, though no such disruption is reported.

watch.what: Any report of Chinese coastguard vessels stopping, boarding or blocking merchant ships near Taiwan or its outlying islands
watch.why: It would show the pressure moving from naval posturing to interference with commercial traffic, which is the route by which India would be affected.

context: India imports many electronic goods and components from East Asia, and much of that cargo passes through the seas around Taiwan. Sustained tension there can therefore matter to Indian supply chains even without any fighting.

escalation.development: Beijing has widened its coastguard patrols around Taiwan, from the eastern approaches to waters near Quemoy and Dongsha Island, and Taipei is shadowing the ships.
escalation.evidence: The reports describe patrols and shadowing only, with no strikes or attacks. This is continued maritime posturing, so the war stays at the level of mobilisation and posturing.

next_signals.signal: Chinese and Taiwanese vessels exchange fire, or one side uses force against the other's ship, such as ramming or firing on it.

events.headline: India's opposition set to hold mega rally seeking election chief's resignation
events.why: India's opposition parties held a large protest in New Delhi demanding the election chief's resignation over a voter list revision that critics fear could leave 130 million voters off the rolls.
implications: If eligible citizens are removed from the voter rolls, they could lose the ability to vote in coming elections, which makes the revision a question of political rights for a very large group.
The protests have been running since the summer and are now backed by a youth movement, the Cockroach Janta Party, which suggests the dispute is drawing in younger voters beyond party members.
Security forces with batons, shields and riot-control vehicles surrounded the protest site, so continuing rallies could disrupt movement and daily business in central Delhi.
The protest is a direct challenge to Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government and the election body, which keeps the fairness of the voter lists at the centre of national politics.

exposure.reason: The dispute reaches Indians through the voter rolls, which decide who can vote, and through protests in Delhi. It concerns political rights and governance rather than household essentials or trade.

horizon.reason: Protests have continued since the summer and the dispute over the revision remains open, so its effects on politics and on Delhi are likely to play out over coming weeks.

confidence.reason: Seven outlets agree that the rally took place, but turnout figures differ and the 130 million figure is a feared exclusion rather than a confirmed count.

watch.what: Any response from the Election Commission of India to demands about the voter list revision
watch.why: It would show whether the election body intends to change the revision or defend it against the opposition's demands.

watch.what: Further opposition rallies or protests by the youth movement in Delhi and other cities
watch.why: It would show whether the protest movement is growing or fading after the Delhi rally.

watch.what: Published figures on how many names were added to or removed from the voter rolls
watch.why: It would show whether the feared exclusion of 130 million voters is borne out.

context: The Election Commission of India is a constitutional body that conducts national and state elections and maintains the electoral rolls; a person must be listed on the roll to vote.
Electoral rolls are revised periodically to add new voters and remove entries for people who have died or moved, and critics often argue that large deletions can exclude eligible citizens.
Rahul Gandhi of the Congress party comes from a political family that has produced three prime ministers and is the main opposition challenger to Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

terms.meaning: A review of the official list of registered voters, in which names are added, corrected or removed.
The head of the Election Commission of India, the body responsible for running elections and maintaining the voter lists.
A youth protest movement that has backed and led demonstrations against the voter list review since the summer.

The protest was against a nationwide revision of voter lists that has fuelled demonstrations since the summer.

explanations.note: The highest figure comes from opposition organisers, who have an interest in a large turnout, while the lower figures come from journalists' own descriptions.
The Guardian figure is an expectation stated before the march, while later reports describe the crowd that actually gathered at different points in the day.
France 24 reported tens of thousands in its morning report and thousands in its evening report, and the reason for the difference has not been given.

chain.detail: A revision of India's voter lists is under way, and critics fear it could leave 130 million voters off the rolls. That fear has fuelled demonstrations since the summer.
Opposition parties led by Rahul Gandhi, backed by the youth Cockroach Janta Party movement, held a large rally in New Delhi demanding the election chief's resignation.
Hundreds of police with batons, shields and riot-control vehicles surrounded the protest site, signalling that authorities expect the confrontation over the voter lists to continue.
If the revision goes ahead unchanged, large numbers of citizens could find themselves unable to vote, and continuing protests could keep disrupting Delhi and national politics.

impact_chain.breaks_if: The effect would stop if the Election Commission alters the revision or eligible voters are shown not to have been removed from the rolls.
